subject: maths

moments.title: Hilbert's 23 problems
moments.who: David Hilbert, International Congress of Mathematicians, Paris
moments.body:
At the 1900 ICM in Paris, Hilbert lists 23 open problems he believes will shape 20th-century mathematics. His broader vision: every mathematical statement is decidable; mathematics can be put on a complete, consistent, formal axiomatic basis.

Many of his problems were solved during the century. The foundational dream — Hilbert's program — was crushed.

quote.text: Wir müssen wissen — wir werden wissen. (We must know — we shall know.)

moments.takeaway: Hilbert sets an agenda. Most of his problems get solved; his deepest hope does not.

moments.title: Principia Mathematica
moments.who: Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead, Cambridge
moments.body:
Russell and Whitehead spend 10 years writing a three-volume work that derives all of basic arithmetic from pure logic. It takes them 379 pages to prove 1 + 1 = 2.

The work is meant to demonstrate that mathematics is reducible to logic (Russell's logicism) and that paradoxes (like the one Russell himself found in 1901) can be avoided. It's largely successful — and almost no one reads it cover to cover.
moments.takeaway: Mathematics is, in principle, derivable from logic. The work is so technical it only convinces other logicians.

moments.title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
moments.body:
Gödel, age 25, publishes 'On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems'. He proves:

1. Any consistent formal system expressive enough to contain arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.
2. Such a system cannot prove its own consistency.

Gödel's method: encode statements about mathematics AS numbers. The system can then 'talk about itself'. He constructs a sentence G that asserts 'G is not provable in this system'.

If the system could prove G, it would prove a false statement — contradiction. If it cannot prove G, then G is true and unprovable.
moments.takeaway: Mathematics has fundamental gaps. There are true things it cannot prove.

moments.title: Turing's halting problem
moments.body:
Independently of Gödel, and using a different approach, Turing proves the halting problem is undecidable: no algorithm can take an arbitrary program and reliably determine whether it will halt or run forever.

In the same paper, Turing defines a 'computable function' — what we now call a Turing machine. He invents theoretical computer science.

Gödel and Turing's results are essentially equivalent (Church-Turing thesis): the limits of formal mathematics are the limits of computation.
moments.takeaway: Computation has fundamental limits. Some questions cannot be answered by any algorithm.

moments.title: Gödel's death
moments.body:
Gödel suffered chronic anxiety and paranoia. He believed his food was being poisoned and would only eat what his wife Adele prepared. When she was hospitalised in late 1977, Gödel stopped eating. He died of starvation in January 1978. His weight at death was 65 pounds.

His Princeton colleagues had tried to help but couldn't. Einstein, who had walked daily with Gödel until his own death in 1955, had said his own work no longer interested him much; he came to the institute mainly to walk home with Gödel.
moments.takeaway: The greatest logician of the 20th century starved himself to death.

now.title: Logic and foundations today
now.body:
We accept that mathematics has provably undecidable problems. The continuum hypothesis, for instance, is independent of ZFC (Gödel 1940, Cohen 1963). Many natural questions in group theory, topology and number theory are similarly independent.

Formal verification, using proof assistants (Coq, Lean, Isabelle), is making computer-checked mathematics increasingly practical. The Liquid Tensor Experiment (2020-2022) had a major recent theorem fully verified by Lean.
now.open_questions: What's the role of undecidability in everyday mathematics? Does P equal NP? (Probably not — but proving it is one of the open Millennium problems.) Can we formalise all of working mathematics so it can be machine-verified? Are there 'natural' true-but-unprovable statements?

reflection: Gödel was Einstein's closest friend in his final years. They walked home together every day. Both made discoveries that overturned the most cherished assumptions of their fields — gravity as geometry, mathematics as incomplete. Both were exiles from Nazi-occupied Europe. What role does the experience of exile and disruption play in the history of foundational thought?
